item.title: AI;DR: Writer advocates for reviewing and editing AI-generated content before sharing to avoid overwhelming readers with unfiltered AI output [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A pro-AI writer expresses frustration with unedited AI-generated text being shared without review, coining the term AI;DR (AI; Didn't Read) as a policy to ignore such content. The writer emphasizes the importance of human editing in AI-assisted writing, especially in professional and social contexts, to maintain clarity and personal touch. The article acknowledges that AI tools are widely used for idea generation and drafting but argues that sharing raw AI output, such as in Slack messages or newsletters, can be off-putting. The writer suggests that while fully AI-generated content may be acceptable in customer support, other communications should be carefully reviewed to ensure quality and authenticity.

item.title: OpenAI cuts GPT-5.6 Sol pricing by 50%
item.description: OpenAI has reduced the price of its GPT-5.6 Sol model by half, making access to this AI model more affordable. This pricing change aims to increase usage and accessibility for developers and businesses leveraging the model for various applications.

item.title: Report: Israel creates fake think tank to influence AI chatbot outputs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Israel reportedly established a fake think tank as part of an effort to manipulate AI chatbots' responses. This tactic appears aimed at shaping the information these models provide by injecting controlled narratives. The creation of the fake entity suggests a strategic attempt to influence AI training data or outputs, raising concerns about the integrity and neutrality of AI-generated information. The implications highlight challenges in ensuring AI systems remain unbiased and resistant to manipulation.

item.title: Wiz Research finds AI-generated GitHub Copilot autofix introduced critical script injection vulnerability in Snowflake's Jira workflow, patched same day [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Wiz Research's AI-powered Red Agent discovered a critical script injection vulnerability in Snowflake's public GitHub repository, introduced by a GitHub Copilot autofix commit on June 18, 2026. The flaw allowed unauthenticated users to execute arbitrary commands in a GitHub Actions runner by submitting a crafted issue title, exposing Jira credentials with read access to Snowflake's internal projects. Snowflake patched the vulnerability and rotated the affected credentials on the same day of disclosure, June 23, 2026, confirming no unauthorized access occurred during the exposure window.

item.title: Guide details how to disable or avoid intrusive AI features across popular software and devices [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A comprehensive guide explains how users can disable or avoid intrusive AI features in various software and devices, including Adobe Acrobat, Android phones with Gemini, Apple devices with Apple Intelligence and Siri, and major web browsers like Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and DuckDuckGo. The guide targets users who prefer less AI interference in their technology environments and provides step-by-step instructions for turning off AI functionalities. The guide covers disabling AI assistants, turning off AI-powered suggestions, and managing AI-related settings in Google Workspace and other platforms. It also includes tips for removing AI enhancements from search results and browser interfaces, aiming to give users more control over their digital experiences without unwanted AI interactions.

item.title: OpenAI releases GPT-5.6 Sol, its most capable vision model with significant improvements in object detection and counting [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI introduced the GPT-5.6 lineup, including the Sol, Terra, and Luna models, with Sol demonstrating the strongest vision capabilities to date. The models were tested on a new vision benchmark covering tasks like object detection, counting, OCR, and data extraction, where Sol notably outperformed previous versions, especially in object detection and counting accuracy. Sol achieved a 46.2 mAP@50 score in object detection, a substantial increase from GPT-5.5's 13.8, and showed strong performance in document layout detection and dense scenes. Counting accuracy also improved, with Sol reaching 73.0% compared to 64.9% for GPT-5.5. OCR and data extraction results were close to prior models, with Sol scoring 90.7% in OCR similarity. Some stability issues were noted with large images, which OpenAI is addressing.

item.title: Researchers present a zero-overhead GPU offload framework integrated into Rust compiler enabling portable, safe, and fast GPU programming across multiple vendors
item.description: A new GPU offload framework built into the Rust compiler and LLVM backends enables high-performance GPU programming with memory safety guarantees, avoiding vendor lock-in and unsafe pointers. The framework leverages Rust's ownership and type systems to optimize data transfers and manages cross-vendor ABI mismatches through a two-pass compilation pipeline. Evaluations on RAJAPerf show that this rustc-based solution generates LLVM IR for GPU kernels that performs competitively against native CUDA and HIP C++ implementations, demonstrating a promising approach for safe and efficient GPU programming in Rust.

item.title: Speko launches OpenRouter for Voice AI, providing a unified API that routes speech models by language and objective based on benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Speko has introduced an OpenRouter platform for Voice AI that integrates multiple speech models into a single API, selecting the best model per language and task using published performance benchmarks. The platform offers a unified gateway with one base URL and API key, compatible with existing frameworks that use the OpenAI API. The service supports various programming environments including LiveKit TypeScript and Python, allowing developers to point their voice AI agents to Speko's gateway without changing their existing code. Speko aims to simplify voice AI development by providing a standardized interface that optimizes model selection and cost efficiency across languages and use cases.

item.title: Report: AI-assisted cheating is widespread among university students, with nearly all using AI tools on take-home exams and assignments [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A recent report from a former university student and professor reveals that nearly every student uses AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini to cheat on take-home exams and assignments. This behavior is widespread and normalized, with students perceiving AI-assisted cheating as easy, harmless, and without stigma. The report argues that the structure of take-home exams and the pressures of academic deadlines contribute to this trend, as students feel encouraged or compelled to use AI to complete their work. It suggests that universities and professors need to acknowledge this reality and reconsider assessment methods, as current approaches fail to prevent or address AI-enabled cheating effectively.

item.title: Un-AI Your Internet: Guide to Reducing AI Integration in Online Services and Regaining User Control [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The article presents a critical view of current large language models (LLMs) and AI technologies, arguing that they rely on predictive algorithms rather than true intelligence. It advocates for users to actively reduce their dependence on AI-infused internet services by disabling or avoiding AI features and applications. It outlines practical steps such as switching away from AI-driven search engines and browsers, and choosing software alternatives without AI components. The piece also contrasts two visions for the internet's future: one controlled by corporations with limited user freedom, and another where users maintain control over their online experience despite increased responsibility for security and customization.

item.title: John Gruber critiques AI text watermarking schemes, questioning their impact on prose quality and transparency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: John Gruber examines recent AI-generated text watermarking methods, arguing that these schemes likely degrade prose quality by introducing predictable randomness that differs from natural language model randomness. He highlights the challenges of embedding detectable signals without affecting meaning and notes that watermarking is less effective for precise text like programming code. Gruber also objects to the secretive nature of current watermarking approaches, which rely on proprietary keys held by AI providers, limiting public verification and raising concerns about transparency and user consent.

item.title: Alibaba launches Qwen3.8-27B, a compact AI model for personal computers, with over one million downloads shortly after release [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Alibaba Group has introduced Qwen3.8-27B, a small AI model designed to run on personal computers. Since its launch, the model has been downloaded more than one million times within a few days, indicating strong early adoption. This development highlights Alibaba's focus on accessible, on-device AI solutions that do not require cloud infrastructure.

item.title: Nvidia shortens AI chip release cycle to one year while assuring older chips retain value amid $150-$200 billion data center deal [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Nvidia is accelerating its AI hardware release cycle from two years to one to encourage rapid adoption of its latest chips, while also assuring customers that older AI chips will maintain their value over time. The company recently partnered with OpenAI and SB Energy to develop an 8-gigawatt data center powered exclusively by Nvidia's next-generation chips, a project CEO Jensen Huang estimates could generate $150 billion to $200 billion in revenue per hardware generation.

item.title: Candy brand discovers TikTok used AI-generated clone of its founder for ads [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A candy brand found that TikTok created an AI-generated clone of its founder to run advertisements on the platform. This incident highlights concerns about the use of artificial intelligence in marketing and issues related to brand representation and consent.

item.title: Researchers find consumers enjoy AI-generated music but preference drops when they learn it is AI-created [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A study by economists and marketing experts at Kiel University and the University of Hamburg found that while listeners generally enjoy music produced by artificial intelligence, their preference declines once they are informed that the music is AI-generated. The research involved three empirical studies exploring consumer attitudes toward AI music and its potential impact on the music industry. The study highlights the growing presence of AI in cultural industries, noting that AI tools like Google's MusicLM can create original music that is difficult to distinguish from human-made songs. The findings raise questions about the future of traditional musicians and the economic dynamics of streaming platforms, where AI-generated content could alter revenue flows and market competition. The research also touches on the ethical and economic implications of AI's role in music production and consumption.

item.title: Anthropic's annualized revenue surges to $65 billion by July, up from $9 billion at end of 2025 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic, an AI model developer, has rapidly increased its annualized revenue run rate to $65 billion by the end of July 2026, up from $9 billion at the end of 2025. This growth outpaces rival OpenAI, which doubled its revenue to $40 billion over the same period. Investors expect Anthropic's revenue to reach between $100 billion and $120 billion by the end of 2026. The company is preparing for a public offering possibly as soon as this fall, aiming for a valuation of $2 trillion or more, which would set a record for the largest market debut.

item.title: Video showcases AI-generated reconstructions of San Diego from 150 years ago [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A new video presents rare visuals of San Diego as it appeared 150 years ago, created using advanced artificial intelligence techniques. These AI-generated reconstructions offer a historical perspective on the city's past, providing viewers with a detailed glimpse into its 19th-century appearance.

item.title: Three independent papers prove 1986 mathematical conjecture using AI, all posted to ArXiv within days [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Three separate research papers were recently uploaded to ArXiv, each presenting a proof of a mathematical conjecture proposed in 1986. All three studies independently used artificial intelligence, including ChatGPT, to assist in their proofs. The papers appeared within days of each other, highlighting concurrent AI-driven advances in mathematical research.

item.title: ScalarDB and ScalarDL launch AI-native features to improve documentation access for humans and AI agents, including conversational search and AI-friendly data formats [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: ScalarDB and ScalarDL have introduced several AI-native enhancements to their documentation sites to improve how both humans and AI agents find and use information. These updates include an Ask AI conversational search interface powered by Google AI Mode, support for English and Japanese queries, and direct URL access to AI search. They also provide llms.txt and llms-full.txt files following the llmstxt.org standard to facilitate AI tool integration and indexing. Additional features include the ability to copy documentation pages as Markdown for easier use in AI tools and editors, and a Chat with page option that lets users start conversations with AI services like ChatGPT, Claude, or Perplexity using the current page context. A GitHub Actions workflow keeps the Context7 library synchronized weekly with the latest documentation content, ensuring AI agents have up-to-date information.

item.title: Tech giants express concerns over AI output quality and seek improvements to reduce misinformation and subpar content [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Major technology companies are raising concerns about the quality and reliability of artificial intelligence outputs, often described as "AI slop." They are working to enhance AI systems to generate more accurate and useful results, addressing challenges related to misinformation and low-quality content generation.

item.title: Google outbids Mercor to acquire Spirit Airlines' corporate data and software for $10 million in bankruptcy auction
item.description: Google won a bankruptcy auction for the internal business data and software code of the collapsed low-cost carrier Spirit Airlines by bidding $10 million, surpassing a $7.5 million offer from Mercor, a company that trains AI models for labs. The acquisition was confirmed in a recent court filing related to Spirit Airlines' bankruptcy proceedings.

item.title: Anthropic plans to add invisible watermarks to Claude-generated text and files to comply with EU AI transparency rules [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Anthropic announced that its AI model Claude will embed invisible watermarks in AI-generated text and attach cryptographically signed metadata to image files to indicate AI origin. This initiative aims to comply with the EU's Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content, which requires clear disclosure when content is AI-produced. The watermarking will apply to all Claude models launched after August 2, 2026, across all platforms, not just in the EU. The watermarks in text will be detectable by AI tools through unique word choice patterns without affecting readability or creativity, and will persist even if the text is copied or lightly edited. For images, the cryptographic signatures in metadata will reveal tampering attempts. Anthropic noted that watermark presence does not guarantee original AI creation, as content can be edited or combined with human-generated text, and complete rewrites may remove the watermark entirely. The company plans to share tools for verifying AI-generated content soon.

item.title: Lullaby Converter uses AI to generate baby-friendly music box versions of any song from uploaded audio files [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Lullaby Converter is a new AI-powered tool that transforms any uploaded song into a gentle music box lullaby suitable for babies, preserving the original melody. Users can upload an audio file, select a favorite segment, and generate a baby-friendly rendition designed to soothe infants.

item.title: AI automation startup Relay shuts down; founder Jacob Bank and staff join Google Chrome team to advance AI integration [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation startup launched in 2021, is shutting down its service with paid customer access ending September 14 and free access already terminated. Founder and CEO Jacob Bank, who previously worked at Google, is rejoining the company as VP of Product for Google Chrome, where he will lead product and developer relations teams. Relay aimed to streamline repetitive business tasks through automation, similar to Zapier, but will now see its team contribute to Google's Chrome browser. Bank indicated plans to enhance AI capabilities within Chrome, describing it as an ideal platform for collaboration with AI agents, aligning with Google's broader integration of AI technologies like Gemini into its products.

item.title: Prime Agent launches an open-source recursive language model agent with self-improving capabilities for long-running coding and research tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Prime Agent is an open-source reinforcement learning-based agent designed to improve its own performance through recursive language modeling and a continual harness that stores and refines supplemental prompts, memories, and skills. It operates within a persistent Python environment, enabling long-running work with features like subagent spawning, autonomous mode, and durable state across sessions. The agent supports programmatic control via IPython, background session persistence, direct agent-to-agent communication, and skill creation from recurring workflows. It is intended for general and long-running research tasks, with mechanisms for evidence-backed refinement and rollback, heartbeat scheduling, and persistent goals to maintain progress over time.

item.title: DOJ investigates Andreessen Horowitz over antitrust concerns related to board seats at competing AI firms Databricks and Fivetran [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The Justice Department is conducting an antitrust investigation into Andreessen Horowitz regarding its board positions at competing artificial intelligence companies Databricks and Fivetran. The probe has been ongoing for nearly a year and coincides with the agency's review of Fivetran's acquisition of dbt Labs. The investigation focuses on potential conflicts arising from Andreessen Horowitz's influence across these competing firms.

item.title: Audit finds large language models prioritize physician reputation and fees over demographic signals in doctor recommendations, with subtle demographic biases undetected by model explanations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted a randomized audit of seven large language models recommending family-medicine physicians based on synthetic profiles varying in reputation, fees, gender, and ethnicity. They found that reputation and fees strongly influenced recommendations, while demographic biases favored female and minority-signaled names over White names, contrary to typical human audit findings. These demographic effects were not reflected in the models' stated reasons, indicating a lack of transparency in self-reported explanations. The audit design allows repeatable evaluation of future models using identical stimuli, suggesting behavioral audits are more effective than self-reports for monitoring AI recommendation fairness.

item.title: Forklane.ai launches a multiplayer coding environment for development teams and agents to collaborate in real time
item.description: Forklane.ai has introduced a new multiplayer coding platform designed to enable real-time collaboration among development teams and agents. The environment aims to improve teamwork efficiency by facilitating simultaneous coding interactions. This platform supports developers working together more effectively by providing shared coding sessions accessible through the web.

item.title: Qwen 3.8 27B scores 52 on Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, matching GPT-5.6 Luna and close to larger models GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Pro [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The Qwen 3.8 27B language model achieved a score of 52 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, equaling the performance of GPT-5.6 Luna and trailing GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Pro by one point. Despite having only 27 billion parameters, Qwen 3.8 27B performs comparably to much larger models, including GLM-5.2 with 753 billion parameters and DeepSeek with 1.6 billion parameters. This result highlights Qwen 3.8 27B's efficiency and competitiveness in the field of generative AI and large language models.

item.title: xAI reports high error rates in grok-4.6 and grok-4.5 models, ongoing monitoring and fixes underway [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The xAI team has identified a high error rate affecting its grok-4.6 and grok-4.5 AI models. The issue is currently being monitored and addressed to improve model performance and reliability.

item.title: Researchers find data selection effects in reasoning fine-tuning depend on model capacity and training duration, with high-likelihood data benefiting smaller models early and low-likelihood data aiding larger models over longer training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied how data selection based on likelihood affects supervised fine-tuning for reasoning tasks, using models from 1.5B to 8B parameters and stronger teacher models. They found a capacity-dependent pattern where high-likelihood data leads to faster early improvements in smaller models, while low-likelihood data becomes more beneficial for larger models with extended training. The study analyzed learning dynamics and proposed a theoretical framework showing that data difficulty, data span, and model capacity jointly influence knowledge transfer. The findings suggest that effective data selection strategies should consider model capacity and computational budget rather than universally favoring high-likelihood supervision.

item.title: Researchers present CForce, a distillation method to improve early-stage prediction consistency in diffusion large language models, enhancing parallel decoding speed and quality [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Consistency Forcing (CForce), a distillation technique designed to align early-stage mask predictions with later stages in diffusion large language models (dLLMs) to reduce errors during aggressive parallel decoding. CForce uses pre-collected self-rollout trajectories and a Confidence Adaptive KL Divergence objective to improve training-inference alignment and minimize early prediction errors. The method applies to both mask-to-token and edit-capable decoding, with experiments on LLaDA models showing improved speed-quality trade-offs under high parallelism. The code is publicly available.

item.title: Researchers find modular cognitive architecture emerges in large language models mirroring human brain networks across language, reasoning, and social tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A study analyzing 46 tasks across language, formal reasoning, social reasoning, and physical reasoning domains finds that large language models (LLMs) develop a modular architecture similar to the human brain's functional specialization. Tasks that engage the same brain networks in humans recruit overlapping neurons in LLMs, while tasks involving different networks recruit distinct neurons. This convergence suggests modularity may be a fundamental property of intelligent systems rather than a biological accident. The research highlights parallels between biological and artificial intelligence architectures despite their different optimization processes, offering insights into the nature of intelligence across systems.

item.title: Researchers present Self-Explainable Latent Reasoning (SELR) framework that enables efficient, interpretable latent reasoning without external decoders for LLMs and VLMs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Self-Explainable Latent Reasoning (SELR), a unified framework that trains a single model to perform latent reasoning while simultaneously decoding its latent representations into human-understandable reasoning steps. This approach addresses the trade-off in existing methods between opaque latent reasoning and reliance on separate decoders, achieving both accuracy and explainability within one model. SELR uses a novel multi-task training objective combining an Answer Loss for accurate final answers and a Chain-of-Thought Loss to generate interpretable reasoning steps. The framework demonstrates improved token efficiency and accuracy over baseline models on both Large Language Models and Vision-Language Models, providing self-contained explainability without architectural overhead or auxiliary models.

item.title: Researchers introduce BCMT, a Blockwise Causal Memory Transformer for long-context language modeling that uses block-level self-attention and exponential causal memory to improve efficiency and reduce memory use [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed BCMT (Blockwise Causal Memory Transformer), a new architecture designed for long-context language modeling that separates local token interactions from global context propagation. BCMT applies dense causal self-attention within local blocks and aggregates adaptive summaries through an exponential causal memory, enabling efficient long-range context propagation without explicit global attention. This approach avoids dense interactions between distant tokens and learned memory states, maintaining compatibility with standard dense self-attention implementations. Experiments with context lengths up to 1024 tokens show that BCMT matches the validation performance of Dense Transformers while significantly improving training throughput and reducing memory consumption. An ablation study confirms that these gains stem from the proposed memory mechanism, demonstrating that exponential causal memory from block summaries offers an effective alternative to dense global attention for long-context language modeling.

item.title: MobileMem introduces a benchmark for on-device long-term memory using a year of mobile user experiences to enable AI agents to learn continuously and adapt [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: MobileMem is a new benchmark and framework designed to study on-device long-term memory for AI agents, based on a year-long collection of mobile user experiences. It aims to support persistent personal assistants that can remember, understand, and learn from heterogeneous, multimodal, and evolving user data over time. The framework uses a knowledge-grounded synthesis pipeline to create coherent, temporally consistent trajectories from user-app sessions, offering text and multimodal settings that involve multi-hop reasoning, knowledge updating, and preference inference. MobileMem shifts AI memory from simple information retrieval toward experiential intelligence for continuous personal learning and adaptation.

item.title: Researchers find no universal signal predicts sample-level regressions in LLM updates across tasks and models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A study analyzing six benchmarks across multiple-choice question answering, math reasoning, and code generation tasks finds that no single inference-time signal consistently predicts when a newer large language model version will perform worse on individual samples compared to its predecessor. The research compares single-model signals like confidence and attention entropy with cross-version signals such as output KL divergence and representation drift, revealing that signal effectiveness varies by task and update pair. Some cross-version signals remain informative even without labels, enabling selective fallback to older models for high-risk samples, and the authors provide code to help practitioners choose appropriate regression signals for specific updates.

item.title: Researchers test internal action maps in pretrained Qwen models, finding state signals decodable without global affine closure [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers evaluated whether internal action maps in pretrained Qwen and Qwen3-4B language models support reusable affine transformations that compose across states. They found that while some geometric and algebraic properties hold in specific layers and finite worlds, global affine closure does not universally apply, indicating separable aspects of state availability, causal use, and local geometry. The study used frozen final-token layers, intervention datasets, and outcome-aware refitting to analyze causal effects and map composition, with results limited to one pretrained model and tested function classes.

item.title: Researchers find reasoning-oriented training amplifies some behaviors in AI models but not those most predictive of correctness across text and vision-language tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers analyzed 15,282 reasoning traces from 15 models across six benchmarks in text-only and vision-language tasks to identify which reasoning behaviors correlate with correct answers and how training affects these behaviors. They introduced Behavioral Lift, a metric measuring the impact of specific behaviors on model correctness, revealing a gap where training amplifies behaviors like self-correction and uncertainty acknowledgment but not the highest-lift behaviors such as confidence calibration and knowledge alignment. The study suggests that current reasoning-oriented training may improve the appearance of deliberation without enhancing the most predictive reasoning behaviors, highlighting the need for training objectives that prioritize calibrated and grounded reasoning over surface-level features.

item.title: Researchers develop SocialRL to train social reasoning in a 4B parameter language model, achieving negotiation performance matching or exceeding GPT-5 across six domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present SocialRL, a training approach that enhances social reasoning in a 4B parameter language model to improve its ability to negotiate and act strategically on behalf of users. The model was trained and evaluated across six domains including Deal-or-No-Deal, Job Interview, and Marketplace, demonstrating performance that matches or surpasses GPT-5 family models in negotiation tasks. The approach leverages in-domain training, cross-domain transfer guided by game structure, and techniques like cascade reinforcement learning and multi-teacher on-policy distillation to consolidate domain specialists into a unified model.

item.title: Researchers propose ACID-compliant framework for autonomous AI agents to ensure reliable execution and consistent outcomes in dynamic environments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce the concept of agentic transactions and an ACID-compliant framework for large language model agents that execute long-horizon tasks autonomously. The framework adapts classical database ACID properties into semantic guarantees-Semantic Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability-to address challenges in reliable execution, concurrency, and state management amid model uncertainty and dynamic workflows. To demonstrate this approach, the team developed an ACID-compliant data agent employing transactional exploration, validation cycles, and semantic state management. Experimental results on standard benchmarks show a 10.6% performance improvement over leading agents, including Claude Code. This work lays the foundation for building trustworthy, scalable, and self-evolving AI agent systems by extending transactional principles to autonomous AI workflows.

item.title: Researchers present Regime-Conditional Verification to adapt and monitor safety classifiers for large language models without retraining, improving policy adherence and detecting distribution shifts [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Regime-Conditional Verification (RCV), a lightweight wrapper that adapts existing safety classifiers used with large language models by estimating the probability that predictions disagree with the deployer's policy and selectively correcting likely errors. RCV also provides a label-free signal to detect distribution shifts, enabling maintenance updates to the correctness estimation layer and reserving classifier fine-tuning for only necessary cases. Across multiple classifiers and datasets, RCV improved adherence to deployer policies and detected all tested attack campaigns in deployment studies. This approach allows ongoing adaptation and monitoring of safety classifiers without frequent retraining, addressing challenges of policy mismatch and performance degradation over time.

item.title: Researchers release Principle-Bench, a four-axis benchmark evaluating LLMs as judges in principle-based regulation with 168 cryptoasset scenarios and introduce Ceca for calibrated assessment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed Principle-Bench, the first benchmark assessing large language models (LLMs) as judges in principle-based regulation across four axes: accuracy, paraphrase robustness, adversarial robustness, and calibration. The benchmark includes 168 cryptoasset financial-promotion scenarios mapped to two UK FCA principles, with paraphrase, adversarial keyword-stuffing, and boundary perturbations created under a pre-registered rubric. They also introduce Ceca (Calibrated Exemplar-Cluster Assessment), a calibrated and auditable assessor that provides exact per-exemplar counterfactual attributions. Testing across keyword counting, sentence-transformer embedders, an open-weight LLM-judge, and a calibrated cascade showed no method excelled on all four axes. A 120-billion-parameter LLM-judge performed well on benign inputs but lost 47 accuracy points on keyword-stuffed Consumer Duty inputs, indicating vulnerability to adversarial manipulation. A second judge from a different model family showed low agreement on these inputs, suggesting the failure stems from the model rather than the dataset. The researchers conclude that deployment-grade LLM-judges for principle-based regulation must report adversarial deception and post-hoc calibration metrics alongside aggregate accuracy.

item.title: Researchers find that wrong answers in multi-agent reasoning can still improve downstream problem solving across multiple benchmarks and models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Diverse Hypothesis Deliberation (DHD), a protocol that measures the trajectory value of messages in multi-agent reasoning by replaying downstream solvers with different message availabilities. Their experiments on five mathematics and science benchmarks using two large language models show that wrong answers can contain useful reasoning components that help improve final outcomes in over 40% of cases where the wrong answer changes correctness. The study finds that retaining the full message, including its reasoning, yields better results than keeping only the answer portion, indicating that answer correctness alone does not determine a message's value. The researchers demonstrate that repeated trajectory-value evidence provides a more effective criterion for deciding which messages to keep or remove than relying solely on answer correctness. Their findings suggest that multi-agent systems can benefit from considering the broader utility of messages beyond correctness, and DHD offers reusable labels to guide learning when agents should incorporate or discard information.

item.title: Researchers propose separating evidence interpretation from decision aggregation in language model systems using a four-field evidence tuple to address count-scale drift and improve reliability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose a framework that separates evidence interpretation from decision aggregation in systems using language models to draw conclusions from multiple sources. They introduce a four-field evidence tuple consisting of hypothesis, reliability bucket, rationale, and provenance, which clarifies the interface between interpreting sources and combining interpretations. This separation reveals a failure mode called count-scale drift, where thresholding sums of unnormalized weights shifts with the number of sources and reader reliability, causing inconsistencies in decision rules. The team addresses these issues by pooling calibrated log-likelihood ratios, an arithmetic fix applicable beyond language models to other additive scoring systems. They demonstrate the approach on a longitudinal corpus, achieving improved performance with a small sequence encoder and tree ensemble compared to a hand-crafted baseline. The framework distinguishes transferable components from those needing domain-specific re-estimation and outlines predictions and negative results to test its validity.

item.title: ShortOPD introduces a short-to-long on-policy distillation method to recover compressed large language models, improving generation quality and training efficiency [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Structured pruning compresses large language models (LLMs) but often degrades their free-form generation capabilities despite maintaining performance on multiple-choice tasks. ShortOPD addresses this by using a short-to-long on-policy distillation schedule that focuses training on effective rollout lengths, avoiding repetitive suffixes confirmed by a frozen teacher model. This approach significantly improves the compressed model's generation scores across math, code, and open-ended tasks, achieving up to nine times the unrecovered performance and reducing training time and rollout tokens compared to standard recovery methods. ShortOPD reallocates training resources to the parts of the rollout that the compressed model can effectively learn from, accelerating loss reduction and matching longer rollout horizons with less computational cost. This method aims to advance structured pruning beyond marginal improvements on perplexity and multiple-choice benchmarks toward deployment-ready generation quality in compressed LLMs.

item.title: Researchers propose CoDE-Stop, an early stopping method using confidence dynamics to reduce computation in large reasoning models by 25-50% without extra training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce CoDE-Stop, a method that monitors confidence changes in intermediate answers to decide when large reasoning models should stop generating chain-of-thought outputs, aiming to reduce computational cost and avoid performance degradation from overthinking. The approach requires no additional training and integrates easily with existing models. Evaluations across multiple reasoning and science benchmarks show CoDE-Stop achieves better accuracy-compute tradeoffs compared to prior early stopping methods, cutting total token usage by 25-50%. The study also analyzes confidence dynamics, revealing that correct reasoning paths reach high confidence early while incorrect ones produce longer, less reliable traces.

item.title: Researchers present PhoneWorld, a pipeline to scale controllable phone-use agent environments from real GUI data across 34 apps and 16 domains [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: PhoneWorld is a reusable system that converts real mobile GUI trajectories and screenshots into controllable environments, executable tasks, automatic verifiers, and training rollouts for phone-use agents. It builds mock Android apps with mutable state and derives tasks and verifiers from real user interactions, covering common mobile behaviors like search, shopping, and social interaction. In evaluations, PhoneWorld supervision improved performance across four benchmarks compared to an AndroidWorld baseline, with gains up to 52.5 points. The study also found that increasing supervision and expanding app coverage further enhanced performance, shifting the focus from building individual mobile benchmarks to scaling the supply of phone-use environments for training agents.

item.title: Don't Claim Benchmark-Oriented Optimization Improves General Coding Capability -- Diverse Evaluation Is Required [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.13566v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training papers, model cards, and blog posts often treat scores on a small set of coding benchmarks (e.g., SWE-bench and LiveCodeBench) as evidence of broad coding capability, both for research artifacts and user-facing systems. We argue that optimization for these benchmarks leads to measuring task-specific performance, creating a meaning gap between measured scores and claims of general coding ability. We examine this gap with a Django-based case study benchmark suite we create. Evaluating foundation models and checkpoints post-trained on SWE-bench trajectories, we find that benchmark rankings frequently fail to generalize. Post-trained checkpoints show little cross-task transfer, and SWE-bench optimization yields limited or no gains on our tasks or on LiveCodeBench. Similarly, fine-tuning on individual Django modalities fails to transfer. We conclude that a small number of benchmarks is insufficient for evaluating diverse models under benchmark optimization pressure. We encourage the community to use differentiated evaluation - holistic assessment for frontier models, multi-task suites for research, and human-in-the-loop studies for narrow task applications. Finally, we argue for creating a capability taxonomy and sustained benchmark maintenance, rather than one-off benchmark releases. Without reliable evaluation standards, engineers and researchers using LLMs and agents have to rely on insufficient evidence to make research, development, and deployment decisions.

item.title: Training-Free Knowledge Transfer Across Model Scales through Activation-Guided Pruning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.13596v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Heterogeneous model fusion seeks to combine models that differ in tasks, initializations, architectures, or scales. We study an underexplored cross-scale setting: improving a small recipient language model with a stronger donor despite substantial architectural mismatch. We ask whether useful capabilities can be transferred without explicit neuron-wise semantic alignment. Building on the observation that truncating a large model to a smaller architecture and injecting it with a tiny mixing weight can already improve the recipient, we propose Activation-Prune-Merge (APM), an activation-guided framework for cross-scale fusion. APM constructs task-conditioned activation maps on the donor, selects salient layers, hidden dimensions, attention heads, and MLP neurons to prune it to the recipient architecture, and injects the resulting donor slice into the original recipient using a micro interpolation coefficient. This formulation treats the donor as a source of concentrated functional components rather than requiring precise structural transplantation. Across 16 benchmarks spanning reasoning, mathematics, code generation, instruction following, and classification, APM improves the overall average accuracy from 55.5% to 60.6% over the original 3B recipient. RTE accuracy increases from 64.3% to 82.3%, QNLI from 52.3% to 65.7%, and BoolQ from 70.8% to 79.2%. Analyses of injection ratios and sequential multi-stage fusion further suggest that activation-guided extraction improves the quality of the transferable donor slice while preserving the small-ratio fusion regime. These results provide evidence that cross-scale heterogeneous fusion can succeed without explicit semantic alignment when the donor contribution is sufficiently concentrated and carefully selected.

item.title: From BERT to Frontier Agents: Eight Years of Language-Model Progress, the Collapse of the Capability-Cost Curve, and the Rise of Task-Targeted Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.13675v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Between October 2018 and July 2026 AI models progressed from simple systems like BERT to massive agents that solve complex math and write software. The ability to resolve real coding issues improved by nearly six times per year since late 2024. During this time costs dropped sharply with OpenAIs budget model GPT 5 point 6 Luna matching flagship capabilities for just one to six dollars per million tokens beating older versions at a fraction of the price. Top performance is now split across specialized models as Claude Opus 5 leads in frontend coding Claude Fable 5 excels at repository level coding and GPT 5 point 6 Sol dominates terminal tasks. In a grade school math test using the Qwen 2 point 5 model basic methods solved 58 of 100 problems while advanced sampling solved up to 79. A confidence ranking tool correctly identified 47 right answers in its top 50 choices proving highly useful for sorting tasks with all research materials made fully public.

item.title: SAGE: Surrogate-gradient Adaptation via Attention-Guided Entropy for Spiking Transformers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.13702v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer an energy-efficient alternative to conventional deep neural networks by exploiting sparse event-driven computation, but their training remains challenging because the non-differentiable spike function requires surrogate gradients whose fixed shape may be suboptimal across layers and training stages. In this work, we introduce SAGE, an uncertainty-modulated surrogate-gradient mechanism for Transformer-based SNNs. SAGE estimates block-level uncertainty from normalized self-attention entropy and uses this signal to adapt the surrogate-gradient slope during training while leaving the inference model unchanged. By modulating only the training-time surrogate parameter, the proposed method preserves the original architecture and deployment cost while improving optimization flexibility. Experiments on CIFAR-10/100 demonstrate that SAGE achieves improved accuracy over fixed-surrogate baselines, with results up to 1-2\% consistent gains across multiple simulation time steps. These results highlight the potential of attention-derived uncertainty as a lightweight training signal for adaptive surrogate-gradient learning in transformer-based SNNs.

item.title: CutClean: Neural Network Pruning for Privacy-Preserving Inference [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.13773v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural networks are increasingly deployed in high-stakes applications with growing privacy leakage concerns. We show that this privacy leakage can occur even in the absence of representation imbalances that lead to traditional dataset biases. This poses significant privacy risks when deploying models that process sensitive attributes. In this context, we propose CutClean, a privacy-aware pruning method that allows to reduce privacy information flow through the network, while increasing its sparsity. Our approach employs auxiliary linear privacy heads placed at each network's block to quantify information leakage, and further applies increasing levels of sparsity to remove the private attribute leakage, measured in terms of the accuracy of the privacy head attached to the last block. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach effectively minimizes private information flow while achieving high sparsity rates and preserving classification target accuracy.

item.title: PPAPlace: Differentiable Cross-Stage Objectives for Chip Placement Optimization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.13790v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Macro placement significantly affects a chip's post-route performance, power, and area (PPA). Most placement methods optimize half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL) as the primary objective. However, recent benchmarking shows a near-zero correlation between HPWL and post-route timing metrics such as the worst negative slack (WNS) and total negative slack (TNS). As a result, all six evaluated artificial intelligence (AI) placers degraded PPA relative to the hierarchical baseline. Recent efforts have tried to train cross-stage predictors to close this gap. However, existing methods focus on macro-only representations and use pre-route metrics as training labels. A label fidelity study of ten circuits at four design flow stages reveals that HPWL and pre-route timing poorly reflect final post-route timing rankings. In contrast, post-global-routing achieves the best balance between final timing fidelity and label generation cost-effectiveness. Based on this finding, PPAPlace is a timing-driven differentiable surrogate predicting post-route PPA from macro and standard-cell placements. The surrogate is a dual-stream predictor that combines graph attention over the chip netlist with spatial convolution over the placement grid. It is trained on post-global-routing labels. The predicted WNS and TNS gradients flow end-to-end back to cell coordinates. PPAPlace exploits these gradients in two ways: as a co-objective injected into an analytical placer's optimization loop (PPAPlace-CoOpt), and as a post-placement refinement step that adjusts macro positions via projected gradient descent (PPAPlace-Refine). On five ChiPBench test circuits excluded from training, PPAPlace improves average WNS and TNS by 22\% and 51\% over the hierarchical baseline while preserving power and routability, using the same predictor without test-circuit retraining. Code is available at https://github.com/ValleyC/PPAPlace.

item.title: Federated Prompt Learning: A Unified Framework, Empirical Analysis, and Future Directions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.13844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become core components of cloud-based intelligent services in academia and industry, yet their training and deployment are hindered by high computational costs, data centralization, and privacy concerns. Federated learning (FL) offers a decentralized training paradigm that enables clients to collaboratively train a learning model without sharing raw data, making it a promising solution for privacy-preserving LLM training and reasoning. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of federated prompt learning (FPL) to review recent advances in integrating the federated learning paradigm and large language models, answering the following research questions: RQ1: The fundamental motivations, characteristics, and enabling technologies of FPL, and how it differs from conventional FL and full-model federated fine-tuning; RQ2: The trade-offs FPL approaches exhibit in performance, communication efficiency, computational overhead, scalability, personalization, and heterogeneity handling; RQ3: The remaining security, privacy, robustness, and system challenges, along with key future research directions. To this end, we systematically examine existing FPL methods across the full model lifecycle: pre-training, fine-tuning, and practical applications, while discussing security, privacy, and robustness issues and summarizing existing defense mechanisms. Finally, we highlight open challenges and future directions, aiming to help readers understand how the insights drive research in FPL.

item.title: Geometric Filtering of LLM-Generated Samples for Few-Shot Text Classification [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.13866v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate synthetic training data for text classification, but the quality of generated samples is heterogeneous: some fall in correct class regions of the embedding space while others land in peripheral or cross-class zones. We propose a geometric filtering framework that evaluates each LLM-generated sample by its Euclidean distance to real class examples in a sentence embedding space, selecting only geometrically consistent candidates. A soft weighting mechanism transforms filter scores into sample weights for classifier training. Evaluated across 13 datasets, 5 classifiers, 10 augmentation methods, and over 6,700 configurations, our method achieves +2.61 percentage points (pp) over SMOTE ($p<0.0001$, Cohen's $d=0.95$, 88.9% win rate). The approach generalizes to named entity recognition (+9.26pp, 100% win rate) without filter modification, and is robust across 5 LLMs from 4 providers. A key finding is that the simplest distance-based filter consistently outperforms complex multi-criteria alternatives.

item.title: Hybrid Quantum-inspired Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Privacy-Aware Federated Biosignal Learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.13914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings are sensitive biomedical data, limiting the ability of hospitals and wearable devices to share raw signals for centralized model training. Federated learning addresses this practical privacy constraint by enabling collaborative model training while keeping raw biosignal data at their respective sources. However, federated ECG classification remains challenging due to limited client-side samples, imbalanced arrhythmia labels, and non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data across clients. These constraints require classifiers that are both communication-efficient and robust to cross-client distribution shifts. In this work, we evaluate a hybrid quantum-inspired Kolmogorov-Arnold network (HQKAN) against a multilayer perceptron (MLP) for five-class arrhythmia classification on the MIT-BIH dataset and three-class classification on the INCART dataset under federated averaging (FedAvg). Across multiple client configurations, HQKAN improves most aggregate and minority-class metrics while using 37.35% fewer trainable parameters and reducing communication cost by 24.89% on MIT-BIH; on INCART, it achieves corresponding reductions of 44.81% and 36.41%. These results indicate that HQKAN offers a compact, communication-efficient and robust alternative to the MLP baseline for privacy-aware federated learning on biosignal data.

item.title: QUASAR: Lowering the Loss Floor of Quantization-Aware Training with Loss-Aware Reconstruction [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.13966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language model inference shifts toward lower precision, post-training quantization (PTQ) becomes increasingly brittle, making quantization-aware training (QAT) essential for preserving model quality. However, QAT computes the loss and surrogate gradients using a lossy reconstruction of latent full-precision weights, while applying updates to the latent weights themselves. This mismatch can lead to suboptimal training trajectories and a higher loss floor. Second-order PTQ methods mitigate a similar gap by minimizing loss-aware reconstruction error, but doing it once for a frozen model can take hours; repeating this process throughout QAT as the weights evolve is impractical. We introduce QUASAR, a QAT method that continuously performs lightweight, loss-aware reconstruction in the training loop to lower the loss floor and improve the resulting low-bit model. At each training step, QUASAR uses the exponential moving average of squared gradients as online saliency estimates, searches over a small set of clipping ranges, and fits affine dequantizers via saliency-weighted least squares. Our analysis shows that the loss-aware reconstruction error is the only reconstruction-dependent term in the QAT convergence bound and controls the loss of the final quantized model, establishing QUASAR's objective as a principled optimization target. QUASAR modifies only the training procedure and supports standard deployment formats, including integer quantization and NVFP4, with no inference-time changes or overhead. Across Qwen3 and Llama-3.1, QUASAR achieves the lowest held-out KL divergence among competitive QAT methods at 2, 3, and 4 bits, reducing KL by at least 10% at 3 and 4 bits and by 29% at 2 bits. At 2 bits, it improves average accuracy across eight tasks by 3.5-4.3 percentage points over strong QAT and PTQ baselines.

item.title: Forecast Collapse in Time-Series Foundation Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.14106v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When forecasting hourly returns for 1,000 US equities, we observe an unexpected phenomenon: predictions become nearly flat and show poor stock ranking, as measured by cross-sectional correlation. We call this forecast collapse. Surprisingly, the phenomenon largely disappears when forecasting trading volume under the same setting. We investigate forecast collapse across time-series foundation models (TSFMs), twelve deep-learning forecasting models, and 97 public benchmark configurations, and find that it is closely tied to target predictability. We identify two distinct reasons behind it: low predictability limits the amplitude of calibrated point forecasts, while per-series objectives leave cross-series structure unidentified. These findings reveal a calibration-ranking tradeoff: optimizing squared error leads to flat predictions, whereas directly optimizing cross-sectional correlation improves ranking but can inflate forecast amplitude by more than an order of magnitude. To address this tradeoff, we introduce CalibRank, a simple objective that balances calibration and ranking. On Finance1K, CalibRank nearly triples cross-sectional correlation while keeping amplitude close to the target, and improves correlation on all tested models. Our results reveal a blind spot in conventional time-series evaluation: per-series metrics can hide failures in cross-series structure needed by downstream decisions.

item.title: From Fixed Grids to Moving Particles:A Transferable Latent Operator for Fluid Dynamics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.14120v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lagrangian modeling is vital to fluid dynamics, as it characterizes particle transport and complements the Eulerian representation. However, Lagrangian trajectories are less commonly available than Eulerian fields, while most neural operators are trained and evaluated primarily in the Eulerian representation. This mismatch motivates a new learning problem: can a model trained solely on Eulerian observations generalize zero-shot from Eulerian field prediction to Lagrangian particle rollout, without Lagrangian supervision or task-specific adaptation? To address this problem, we propose the Transferable Latent Operator (TLO), which learns a unified flow representation shared by Eulerian field prediction and Lagrangian particle rollout. TLO decouples latent flow evolution from coordinate-dependent decoding: querying the evolving latent representation at fixed spatial coordinates yields Eulerian fields, whereas querying velocities at particle positions and recursively updating these positions enables Lagrangian rollout. Across five fluid-dynamics benchmarks, TLO consistently outperforms existing neural operators in both Eulerian field prediction and zero-shot Lagrangian rollout, with further gains from limited Lagrangian fine-tuning.

item.title: Overcoming Shortcut Learning in Graph Neural Networks through Active Explanation Guidance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.14121v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) can solve prediction tasks by unintentionally exploiting shortcuts---that is, edges, nodes, and features that correlate with but are not causal for the prediction---which compromise their reliability in out-of-distribution tasks. We introduce XIGL, an architecture-agnostic human-in-the-loop strategy for removing such shortcuts from GNNs. Our key insight is twofold. On the one hand, reliance on shortcuts can be detected by inspecting GNN explanations. On the other hand, once made aware of such shortcuts, sufficiently expert users can provide tailored corrective feedback, which helps deconfound the model. XIGL supports any query strategy; however, since corrective feedback can be expensive to acquire, we develop an active learning strategy for prioritizing explanations that are more likely to display shortcut behavior, lowering annotation and cognitive costs. We showcase the effectiveness of XIGL, including both existing and proposed explanation-based strategies, on several GNN architectures. Our implementation is available online.

item.title: Structure-Guided Spatiotemporal Attention Graph Neural Network for Traffic Flow Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.14177v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep spatiotemporal models integrating graph convolutions and attention mechanisms have demonstrated excellent performance in network-level traffic flow prediction, owing to their exceptional ability to capture complex spatiotemporal dependencies. Despite their predictive success, deployment of such models in safety-critical urban systems remains constrained by their inherent lack of transparency. Existing post-hoc diagnostic methods often struggle with spurious correlations and fail to unveil the intrinsic decision-making mechanisms governing traffic dynamics, resulting in suboptimal interpretability and limited operational trustworthiness. To address these challenges, this paper proposes the Structure-Guided Spatiotemporal Attention Graph Neural Network (SGSAN). Departing from traditional architectures that rely on unconstrained adaptive graphs, SGSAN explicitly learns a static Directed Dependency Graph (DDG) to identify the invariant macroscopic propagation paths of traffic states. We further introduce an InfoNCE-based soft-coupling mechanism that anchors the model's dynamic spatiotemporal attention to this structural prior, offering a mechanistic account of the model's decision-making process while ensuring robust forecasting by aligning attention-based reasoning with identified macroscopic dependencies and preventing over-reliance on ephemeral local noise. Furthermore, a decoupled two-stage optimization framework is developed to resolve the fundamental conflict between structural discovery and predictive error minimization. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that SGSAN achieves state-of-the-art predictive accuracy while providing built-in interpretability that organically aligns with the physical logic of traffic networks.

item.title: KV Cache Compression Through the Lens of Transform Coding [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.14191v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The key-value (KV) cache stores information from past tokens and is a major memory bottleneck in long-context inference. Existing quantization methods address this bottleneck by representing the KV cache uniformly with lower-precision data types and designing quantization schemes to minimize reconstruction error in the cache itself, without accounting for how that error propagates through attention mechanisms. We prove that, under a white-noise quantization model, the expected attention-aware distortion decomposes into additive key and value contributions that factor across tokens and channels. Building on transform coding and reverse water-filling, which are classical tools from signal processing and rate-distortion theory, we introduce Attention-Aware Transform Coding (AATC), which allocates bits over a calibration set to minimize attention-aware distortion. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, evaluated across LongBench, RULER, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, and MATH-500, our method achieves near-lossless accuracy at approximately $5.8\times$ compression, whereas each baseline degrades in at least some settings.

item.title: MINT: A Universal Zero-Shot Predictor for Transaction Data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.14198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Banks analyse sequential financial transaction data to perform many tasks, including fraud prevention, credit risk assessment and offer personalization. To improve the predictive accuracy of these tasks, Payments Foundation Models encode transaction sequence data as rich contextual embeddings, which can then be provided to task-specific models as features. However, these Foundation Models are not designed for flexible zero-shot reasoning across novel downstream prediction tasks, limiting their adaptability and utility. Existing LLM-based approaches to zero-shot prediction often fail to fully exploit the predictive signal within transaction data, while relying on costly text serialization or task-specific architectures that scale poorly. To address these limitations, we present the Multimodal Instruction Network for Transactions (MINT), a framework that connects a pretrained transaction sequence encoder to a decoder-only LLM through lightweight embedding injection, transaction-language alignment, and instruction tuning. We find that MINT achieves state-of-the-art predictive question-answering performance in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution questions, while substantially reducing input tokens, latency, and memory consumption compared to text-serialization baselines. Through comprehensive analyses of representations, alignment strategies, training data, and history length, we establish that compact transaction embeddings are a superior approach to transaction representation than text serialization for multimodal reasoning and zero-shot prediction tasks.

item.title: Training Fair Tabular Foundation Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.14211v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) have emerged as leading methods for tabular predictive tasks, leveraging in-context learning to predict on new data without task-specific training. Despite the increased use of TFMs in high-stakes decision-making, their fairness properties remain largely unexplored. In this work, we incorporate fairness constraints directly into TFM training, enabling fair predictions in a single forward pass. Our approach addresses two key challenges: limited access to sensitive attributes in training data, and the incompatibility of existing fairness techniques with the in-context learning paradigm. We propose FairTFM, a scalable training strategy based on synthetic fairness tasks and a fairness-aware architecture using a gradient reversal layer, which encourages the model to learn representations invariant to sensitive attributes. Experiments on 132 fairness tasks show consistent improvements in fairness while maintaining competitive accuracy.

item.title: Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization for Model Merging [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.14264v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model merging combines trained models directly in weight space, offering a compute-efficient alternative to additional fine-tuning. Selecting merge parameters is nevertheless difficult because downstream evaluations are expensive, gradients are unavailable, and source capabilities can conflict. We formulate merge-parameter selection as a black-box multi-objective optimization problem and introduce MOBO-Merge, a merge-operator agnostic framework that uses multi-objective Bayesian optimization to approximate the Pareto front under a limited evaluation budget. We evaluate Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B in two-model instruction-math and three-model instruction-math-code settings using Linear, SLERP, TIES, and block-wise merge operators. On held-out benchmark partitions, MOBO-Merge obtains higher mean hypervolume than random search in 11 of 12 reported comparisons. The gain is small for one-dimensional Linear interpolation but substantially larger for several TIES, block-wise, and three-objective searches. No merge operator is uniformly best: TIES leads in three of four family-setting combinations, whereas Block-Linear 4x is strongest for the Llama three-model merge. These results show that multi-objective Bayesian optimization is valuable as a search layer for expressive merge parameterizations.

item.title: Mind the Long Tail: Understanding the Difficulty of Delay Detection in Business Processes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.14367v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The early detection of delayed cases in business processes is a critical capability for organizations. Predictive process monitoring (PPM) supports this task by using historical event logs to predict the remaining time of ongoing cases, enabling timely interventions to avoid missed deadlines and service level violations. Although remaining time prediction has advanced considerably through sophisticated deep learning architectures, little is known about the intrinsic difficulty of delay detection itself. Since performance is typically assessed using aggregate metrics, prior work provides limited insight into how models perform across the target distribution, especially on the operationally most critical cases with large delays. In this paper, we address this gap by analyzing the difficulty of delay detection. Across 14 event logs, we show that remaining times are typically strongly right-skewed, with only a small fraction of cases exhibiting large delays. Existing models capture the mode of this distribution well but perform poorly on high-delay cases. We further uncover pronounced heteroscedasticity, showing that predictive uncertainty increases with delay magnitude. Based on these findings, we evaluate approaches to mitigate the imbalance problem, but find only limited benefits, suggesting that the key underlying problem may not be imbalance but higher uncertainty associated with delayed cases. We show that this correlation can be exploited to substantially improve the identification of delayed cases. Overall, our work provides new insights into the sources of difficulty in delay detection and identifies uncertainty-aware modeling as a promising direction for future PPM research.

item.title: DeaMoE: Efficient MoE Structure for Fast Small-Batch Decoding [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.14385v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have been widely adopted in real-time interactive applications such as coding assistants, real-time audio-video interaction systems. To meet the extremely low response latency requirements of these scenarios, practitioners commonly employ small-batch decoding, under which MoE inference becomes memory-bound and is severely bottlenecked by expert weight loading. However, this bottleneck has received limited attention, and existing solutions such as post-training weight compression or fine-grained expert design during pre-training either degrade model accuracy or introduce additional computation and communication overhead. To tackle this issue, we propose DeaMoE, a decoding-efficient MoE architecture, in which the experts are grouped into several departments, and the experts belonging to the same department share most parameters since they come from the same professional field, and additionally each expert contains a few private parameters to reflect its uniqueness. Moreover, we design customized two-stage routing strategy for DeaMoE to avoid redundant loading, under which DeaMoE greatly improves the efficiency during LLM decoding. Compared with vanilla MoE, DeaMoE reduces per-step loaded weights by up to 50.9% and achieves up to 1.33 end-to-end TPOT speedup for the pre-trained 7B model on A40, and up to 2.00x and 1.97x peak speedup for DeepSeek-V3 on A40 and H100 in microbenchmarks.

item.title: Designing Compact Neural Architectures via Neuron Gating and Mixed Activation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.14443v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) is naturally formulated as a bilevel optimization problem, where the upper-level optimizes the architecture using validation performance and the lower-level trains network parameters using training loss. However, NAS is computationally expensive due to discrete architectural decisions, exponentially growing search spaces, and the high cost of training candidate architectures. This work develops a general bilevel optimization framework for NAS across diverse architectures, including MLPs, CNNs, RNNs, and Transformers, to identify compact architectures with strong predictive performance. We propose three scalable formulations that replace discrete neuron- and activation-level decisions with continuous relaxations, enabling differentiable optimization over otherwise combinatorial architecture spaces. These formulations give rise to three NAS methods: NAS based on Neuron Gating (NAS-NG), NAS based on Mixed Activation (NAS-MA), and NAS based on Neuron Gating and Mixed Activation (NAS-NGMA). Experiments on MLPs and CNNs using MNIST and CIFAR-10 show that the proposed methods consistently identify compact architectures with competitive or improved predictive performance. On MNIST, NAS-NGMA achieves 98.68% test accuracy with 7.69M MLP parameters, while NAS-NG achieves 99.63% accuracy with only 0.26M CNN parameters. On CIFAR-10, the proposed methods consistently outperform vanilla DARTS. Further experiments demonstrate that NAS-NG can optimize substantially over-parameterized and literature-optimal architectures, improving accuracy while reducing parameters. These results establish relaxed bilevel optimization as a scalable alternative to discrete NAS and provide a general framework for efficient neuron- and activation-level architecture optimization.

item.title: LP-NAS: Linear Programming-based Neural Architecture Search [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.14472v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) aims to automate neural network architecture design, reducing reliance on human expertise. Among the various NAS methods, differentiable NAS has gained prominence due to its efficiency and accuracy compared to conventional NAS approaches. Since differentiable NAS relaxes the architecture search space into a continuous domain, it is possible to apply principles from continuous optimization to NAS. In this paper, we propose Linear Programming-based NAS (LP-NAS), a mathematical programming-based framework for differentiable NAS that is applicable to a wide range of continuous search spaces. LP-NAS formulates a linear program (LP) using the validation-loss gradient and the training-loss Hessian to compute an architecture update direction that improves generalization while preserving the optimality of the model parameters. By following this LP-derived descent direction, LP-NAS efficiently navigates the architecture search space, leading to faster and more effective architecture optimization. We introduce two computationally efficient variants of LP-NAS, namely S-LP-NAS and R-LP-NAS. Applying LP-NAS to the Differentiable Architecture Search (DARTS) search space results in two algorithmic variants, S-LP-DARTS and R-LP-DARTS. Both variants achieve faster convergence and significantly higher validation performance during the early search iterations than the standard DARTS algorithm. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 show that LP-DARTS outperforms standard DARTS in both the architecture search and evaluation phases. Additionally, we compare our approach with several DARTS variants (P-DARTS, PC-DARTS, and STO-DARTS) on the CIFAR-10 dataset and demonstrate its effectiveness. Furthermore, we validate the transferability of the discovered architectures through experiments on the ImageNet dataset.

item.title: Generating Benchmark Health Data Using a Tabular Diffusion Transformer [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.14496v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cross-Tabular Data Generation (CTDG) seeks to learn a generative model from multiple heterogeneous tables and produce new synthetic tabular datasets. However, existing synthetic tabular data generation methods are largely restricted to single-input-table scenarios and struggle to effectively handle multiple heterogeneous tables with diverse feature sets. To address this limitation, we propose a two-stage framework for cross-tabular data generation. In the first stage, each heterogeneous raw table is transformed into a standardized statistical table with the same set of columns across all tables. Each statistical table captures the marginal distributions of the original columns and the pairwise correlations among them. In the second stage, a diffusion transformer model is trained to capture structural patterns across these homogeneous statistical tables and to generate synthetic statistical tables. Synthetic raw tables are subsequently reconstructed from the generated statistical tables via multivariate Gaussian sampling followed by an inverse probability integral transform. This two-stage CTDG framework enables the learning of a unified generative model from multiple heterogeneous tables and supports the generation of an unlimited number of realistic synthetic heterogeneous tables. Experimental results demonstrate high fidelity in the learned statistical representations and a favorable fidelity-diversity trade-off in the generated synthetic data, validating the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

item.title: RecipeNet: A Hierarchical Transformer for Recipe Data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.14505v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recipe data arises in domains such as materials synthesis, pharmaceutical formulation, and industrial manufacturing, where procedures are represented as ordered sequences of steps containing heterogeneous structured fields. Existing tabular learning methods typically flatten this structure into fixed-schema representations, limiting their ability to capture hierarchical field interactions and procedural dependencies. We propose RecipeNet, a hierarchical Transformer architecture that encodes field-level interactions within each step and sequential dependencies across steps through stacked Transformer encoders. Experiments on multiple recipe datasets and tasks demonstrate that RecipeNet consistently outperforms existing tabular models, highlighting the value of hierarchical and sequential modeling for recipe representation learning.

item.title: Interactive Analysis of Global Explanations using Aggregated Class Activation Maps for Network Data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.13575v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent machine learning (ML) advances have demonstrated that deep learning (DL) achieves impressive results in different application domains, including the classification of computer network traffic to corresponding applications. However, the data frequently contains diverging patterns within a single predicted class. This presents a significant challenge to the ability to provide a clear and comprehensive explanation and emphasizes the necessity for tools capable of detecting and analyzing these patterns. Furthermore, the capacity to extract descriptive rules for classes is a crucial requirement in network traffic analysis and intrusion detection, particularly when leveraging advanced tools like next-generation firewalls. We provide a visual-interactive system that explains predictions of classes for network traffic. Global explanations derived from multiple samples of a given class contribute to understanding model predictions.
